CQ25.brief: A real production has many shots, many takes of each shot, and many people who work on them. A clear structure with fixed names keeps the master sequence safe and easy to read. Unreal can create a master sequence with numbered shots for you. In this quest you create that structure, add takes and notes, test which sequence wins when two of them animate the same light, and write a naming rule for a team.
checklist: In the toolbar, click Cinematics and choose Add Level Sequence with Shots. Name it SEQ_Master. Set Number of Shots to 3, Shot Prefix to sh, Shot Num Digits to 4 and Shot Increment to 10.
Open the first shot (sh0010). Add a Cine Camera, a Camera Cuts section and one keyframed camera move. Do the same for sh0020 and sh0030, each with a different framing.
Right-click sh0020 and choose New Take. Save it in the same folder. Change the camera move in the take. Then open the Takes menu and confirm that the star is on the new take.
Right-click each shot and choose Edit Meta Data. Enter your name, the date and a one-line note. Hover over a shot to see the tooltip.
Give each shot a different Color Tint. Right-click the shot, open Properties and set Color Tint.

Add one light to SEQ_Master (the root sequence) and add the same light to sh0010. Keyframe a different color in each of the two sequences. Right-click sh0010, open Properties and change Hierarchical Bias to -50, then back to 0. Watch which color wins each time.
Write a short naming and folder rule for your team in a text file next to SEQ_Master. It should cover the shot prefix, the number of digits, the take separator and the folder where takes are saved.
CQ25.done_when: Send a screenshot of the SEQ_Master timeline that shows 3 color-tinted shots, the Takes menu open with the star on Take 2, and the metadata tooltip. Also send the text of your naming rule.

CQ26.brief: A render pass is an extra image that holds one kind of information about a frame, such as the distance of each pixel from the camera or which object each pixel belongs to. A compositor, the person who finishes the picture in another program, uses passes to fix or restyle parts of a frame without a new render. In this quest you render a short shot with depth, motion and Object Ids passes into EXR files that hold several layers.
checklist: Open Edit > Plugins and enable Movie Render Queue Additional Render Passes. Restart the editor.
Open Movie Render Queue and add a job for a short shot of 24 to 48 frames from your Scene quest.
Under Deferred Rendering, enable Disable Multisample Effects. In Additional Post Process Materials, enable both MovieRenderQueue_WorldDepth and MovieRenderQueue_MotionVectors.
Add the Object Ids pass and set Id Type to Actor. This pass gives every actor its own mask.
Add the Anti-Aliasing setting. Set Spatial Sample Count to 8, turn on Override Anti Aliasing, and set the method to None.
Remove the other exports. Add EXR Sequence and enable Multilayer. Set File Name Format to {render_pass}/{sequence_name}.{frame_number}.
Render the job. Open the output folder, and open one EXR file in an image viewer or compositing tool that can read layers. Find the Object Ids (cryptomatte), WorldDepth and MotionVectors layers.
CQ26.done_when: Send a screenshot of the MRQ settings list of the job, a screenshot of the output folder with the pass subfolders, and one frame shown with its Object Ids layer or its depth layer visible.

CQ27.brief: The Path Tracer is a render mode that follows the path of light rays through the scene very exactly. It gives lighting that is very close to reality with almost no setup, but each frame takes much longer to render. In this quest you turn the Path Tracer on, render a still frame and a moving shot with it, and compare the result and the render time with the normal renderer.
checklist: Open Project Settings. Set Default RHI to DirectX 12, and enable Support Hardware Ray Tracing and Enable Path Tracing. Accept Support Compute Skin Cache when the editor asks. Restart the editor.
In the viewport, open View Modes and choose Path Tracing. Let the frame converge, which means waiting until the noise is gone. Note how long it takes to become clean.
In your Post Process Volume, open the PathTracing category. Set Max Bounces, Samples Per Pixel and Max Path Intensity. Turn Emissive Materials off and on, and look for places that are lit twice.
Check your materials. Keep the diffuse Base Color below 0.8, and fix any bright white walls.
Create a job in MRQ. Remove Deferred Rendering and add the Path Tracer renderer. For a still frame, use Spatial Sample Count 16 and Temporal 1. Render one frame and note the time.
For a moving shot of 48 frames, use Spatial 1 and Temporal 8, and enable Reference Motion Blur. Render it and note the seconds per frame.
Compare a Path Tracer frame with the same frame rendered with Deferred Rendering. Write three differences that you can see.
CQ27.done_when: Send one path-traced still and one frame from the moving shot, a screenshot of the MRQ settings list, and a short note with the seconds per frame for both renders and the three differences you saw.

CQ28.brief: Every quality setting in Movie Render Queue makes a render take longer, and the costs multiply. Before you start a long render, you should know what each setting costs on your machine. In this quest you render the same 48-frame shot three times with rising quality, measure the time of each render, and write a rule for what fits into one night of rendering.
checklist: Pick a shot of 48 frames with a moving camera and one moving object. Add a Burn In setting, which prints information on the image, so that each frame shows the job name and frame number.
Render A: in Anti-Aliasing use Spatial 1 and Temporal 1, and export a PNG Sequence at 1920x1080. Write down the seconds per frame and the total time.

Render B: use Spatial 1 and Temporal 8, turn on Override Anti Aliasing and set the method to None. Extend your tracks one frame before the start, so that the first temporal sample has data. Note the time.
Render C: use the same settings as B, and add High Resolution with Tile Count 2 and Overlap Ratio 0.1 at 3840x2160. Note the time.
On the shot that has cloth or particles, add Engine Warm Up Count 32 and Render Warm Up Count 8. Compare the first frame with warm-up and without it.
Make a table with these columns: render, settings, seconds per frame, total minutes, and what got better. Add the file name format you used, which must include the {ts_count} and {ss_count} tokens.
Write a budget rule of 3 lines: for a film of 60 seconds at 24 fps, which settings fit into an overnight render on your machine.
CQ28.done_when: Send a writeup with the table for renders A, B and C (seconds per frame and total time), one frame from each render, a comparison of the first frame with and without warm-up, and your budget rule.

CQ29.brief: A shot kit is a folder of ready-made cameras, rigs and render presets that other people can use to build shots quickly. The real test of a kit is that someone else can use it without your help. In this quest you build the kit, make a demo sequence with it, write a README file that explains it, and ask another member to test it.
checklist: Make a folder named Content/ShotKit with the subfolders Cameras, Rigs, Presets and Docs.

Create at least three Camera Animation Sequences, which are reusable camera moves. In the Content Browser, choose Animation, then Camera Animation Sequence. Name them CAS_PushIn, CAS_Handheld and CAS_Orbit. Make CAS_Handheld additive (set Blend Type to Additive) so that it can be layered on any camera.
Build two reusable rig Blueprints: BP_RigRail, a Camera Rig Rail with a Cine Camera attached, and BP_RigCrane, a Camera Rig Crane with a Cine Camera. Expose the useful values as variables.

In MRQ, save two presets. MPC_Final is a Movie Pipeline Master Config with EXR, tone curve off, Spatial 1, Temporal 8, AA None and Burn In. MPC_Preview uses PNG, 1 and 1 samples, and half resolution. Also save one Shot config named MPS_HeroDoF for a shot that needs more spatial samples.

Create SEQ_KitDemo with Add Level Sequence with Shots, with 3 shots. Use a different kit item in each shot: a rig, a Camera Animation Sequence through the Template Sequence track, and CAS_Handheld layered on a rail move. Render it with MPC_Preview, and then render one shot with MPC_Final.

Write Docs/README as a text or markdown file. It says what each asset is, how to add it to a shot, the naming rule from CQ25, which preset to use when, and the expected seconds per frame for each preset on your machine.
Ask another member to follow the README and build one new shot with the kit without your help. Add their feedback and fix the README.
CQ29.done_when: Send the ShotKit folder, the README, the rendered demo (the preview and one final shot), and a note from the other member who tested the kit. A mentor reviews your work.

CQ30.brief: A virtual camera lets you hold a phone or tablet like a real camera and move it by hand, while Unreal moves the camera in the scene in the same way. This gives natural, human camera moves in a few minutes. Live Link is the Unreal system that receives live data, such as this motion, from outside devices. In this quest you connect a device with the Unreal VCam app, check the connection in Live Link, and record a camera take.
checklist: Open Edit > Plugins and enable VirtualCamera, Live Link and Take Recorder. Restart the editor.
Install the Unreal VCam app on an iOS device (version 15 or later, with ARKit) or an Android device (with ARCore). Put the device on the same network as your PC.
In the Place Actors panel, search for VCAM and drag a VCam Actor into your scene. Notice that the viewport starts to pilot it.
Open the Pixel Streaming dropdown (not Pixel Streaming 2) and read the Signaling Server URL that matches your network. Enter it in the app and press Connect.
Walk with the device to frame a shot. Then use the touch joysticks to add extra movement on top of the tracked motion.
Open Window > Live Link. Find the source and the subject for your device, and confirm that the status light is green.
Record a camera take of 10 seconds with Take Recorder and play it back in Sequencer.
CQ30.done_when: Send a screenshot of the Live Link window that shows the connected source and subject with a green light, a screenshot of the recorded take open in Sequencer, and a short clip or screenshot of the view in the VCam app.

CQ31.brief: Every track in Sequencer has controls that protect it or change when it plays. Lock stops a track from being edited, Mute turns a track off, and Solo turns off every other track. A condition makes a track play only in certain cases. In this quest you try each of these controls, add a Fade Track that fades the whole picture to a color, and filter the track list.
checklist: Open a Level Sequence named LS_TrackTour that has at least one camera and two Static Mesh actors. Use Add Track (+), then Actor To Sequencer, to add the meshes.
Right-click one mesh track and choose Rename. Give it a clear name. Notice that the actor in the level gets the new name too.
Right-click the camera track and choose Locked. Try to add a key on it. Then unlock the track again.
Right-click one mesh track and choose Solo. Drag the playhead and watch the other tracks stop working. Then use Mute on one track and see its actor become hidden in the viewport.
Add a Fade Track with Add Track (+), then Fade Track. Key the value 0 at frame 0 and the value 1 near the end. Right-click the fade section, open Properties, and set Fade Color to white.

Right-click one mesh track, open Edit Track, then Condition, and add a Scalability Condition. This makes the track play only at certain quality settings. Turn on Editor Force True so that it still plays in the editor.
Type part of a track name in the Sequencer search field. Then open the Filters menu to filter the list by track type.
CQ31.done_when: Send one screenshot of Sequencer that shows a locked track (with a red border on its keyable tracks), a soloed or muted track, the Fade Track section, and the condition icon on a section. Add one line that says what your Scalability Condition does.

CQ32.brief: Sequencer can animate almost any property of an actor, not only its position. A property is a value in the Details panel, such as the brightness or the color of a light. This is the base for animated lights, materials and gameplay cinematics. In this quest you add property tracks of different types, show a curve inside a track, and add noise to one channel of a transform.
checklist: Create a Level Sequence named LS_Properties. Add a Point Light and a Static Mesh actor to it. Note which tracks appear by default.

On the light, use Add Track (+), then Properties, and add Intensity (a float, which is a number with decimals) and Light Color (a color). Key two values on each track. Double-click a color key to open the Color Picker.
Right-click the Intensity section, open Display, and choose Show Curve. The float curve is now drawn inside the track.
Add a Boolean property, which can only be on or off, for example Visible / Hidden In Game. Key it on and off. Notice the red and green colors on the timeline.
On the Transform track of the mesh, right-click the section, open Properties, and turn on Use Quaternion Interpolation. Set Show 3D Trajectory to Always.
Right-click the Location Z channel of the transform and choose Override with Double Perlin Noise. Change Frequency and Amplitude in Double Perlin Noise Parameters.
Right-click the transform section, open Active Channels, and disable Scale.
CQ32.done_when: Send one screenshot of Sequencer that shows the Intensity track with its curve drawn inside it, the Boolean track with red and green regions, and the Perlin noise channel on the transform. Add one line that says which Amplitude and Frequency you set.

CQ33.brief: The Curve Editor shows each animated value as a line over time, and good motion is shaped there. It has tools that go beyond moving single keys: you can store a copy of a curve, move many keys in time at once, scale groups of keys, and bake a curve into many keys. In this quest you try each of these tools on a simple animated mesh.
checklist: Open LS_Properties or a new sequence. Animate the Location of a mesh with at least five keys. Open the Curve Editor from the Sequencer toolbar.
Select the Location Z track in the Curve Editor Outliner. Press F to Zoom to Fit. Try the three View Modes: Absolute, Stacked and Normalized.
Select one key. Turn on Weighted Tangents and stretch a tangent handle. Hold Shift while you move a tangent to snap it to 45 degrees.
Right-click a curve segment and choose Buffer Curves, which stores a copy of the curve. Move some keys. Then right-click and choose Apply 1 Buffered Curves to go back to the stored curve.
Enable the Retime Tool (Ctrl + E). Double-click in the graph to add an anchor. Drag the anchors to move the keys in time.
Enable the Multi Select Tool (Ctrl + M). Select several keys and scale them with Pivot Type set to First Key.

Open the Filter Tool. Bake the selected keys with Use Frame Bake turned on and Bake Interval in Frames set to 2. Then set Post Infinity to Oscillate (Ping Pong) on the curve, which decides how the curve continues after its last key.
CQ33.done_when: Send two screenshots: one of the Curve Editor in Stacked view with the faint image of a buffered curve visible, and one after baking that shows the dense keys and the Oscillate post-infinity. Add one line that says which tool you found most useful.

CQ34.brief: A section is one block of animation on a track. A track can hold several sections, and they work like layers: an Additive section adds its values on top of the base section. This lets you add noise, offsets and fixes without touching the base keys. In this quest you stack three sections on one track, give them soft starts and ends, change the speed of one with a Time Warp, and choose what happens when the sequence ends.
checklist: Create a Level Sequence named LS_Blends with a mesh that has a Transform track. Right-click the section, open Properties, and unlock Section Range Start and End. The section now has a fixed start and end.
Click Section (+) on the Location track and add a second section with Blend Type set to Additive. Key a small up-and-down move on it and watch it stack on top of the base.
Add a third section with Blend Type set to Additive from Base. Notice that its first key is equal to the current value at that time.
Drag the blend handle at the top corner of a section to make an ease in and an ease out. Right-click the blend curve and set Easing Length to a fixed length. Then choose a curve shape from Options.
Drag two Absolute sections so that they overlap. Drag the playhead through the overlap, and use Order to change which section shows its keys.
On one section, click Add (+), then Add Time Warp, then Time Warp Curve. Key the play rate so that the motion slows down in the middle.
Right-click the base section, open Properties, and set When Finished to Keep State. Play past the end and confirm that the mesh stays in its final position.
CQ34.done_when: Send one screenshot of the Location track that shows at least three sections (Absolute, Additive, Additive from Base) with a visible ease curve and the Time Warp channel. Add one line that says what When Finished set to Keep State changes.

CQ35.brief: In a game, a cutscene often has to use the character that the player controls, and that character does not exist until the game runs. A custom binding solves this. A Replaceable binding shows a preview actor while you edit, and when the game runs it uses a real actor that a function in the Director Blueprint chooses. In this quest you bind a sequence to the player pawn, look at the Blueprint that does the binding, and then remove the binding again.
checklist: In a Third Person project, make a Level Sequence named LS_PlayerBind. Drag the player character Blueprint from the Content Browser into Sequencer, so that it becomes a spawnable preview.
Right-click the character track and choose Convert Selected Binding(s) To…, then Replaceable from Director Blueprint…, then Quick Bind, then Resolve to Player Pawn.
Add a Camera Cut and a short camera move that frames the character. Add an Animation track on the character with any animation.
Place a Level Sequence Actor in the level and turn on Auto Play. Press Play In Editor and confirm that the real player pawn is used, not the preview.

Right-click the track and choose Convert Selected Binding(s) To…, then Replaceable from Director Blueprint…, then Create New Binding Endpoint. Open the Director Blueprint and look at the binding node and its return node.
Split the Return Value struct pin so that you see its parts. Set Return Value Object to an actor you choose, and test with Is Possessed Object turned on and turned off.
Right-click the track, open Binding Properties, and use the trash icon to remove the custom binding. Notice that the Blueprint functions are still there.
CQ35.done_when: Send one screenshot of Play In Editor with the cinematic running on the real player pawn, and one screenshot of the Director Blueprint that shows the Dynamic Binding node with its split Return Value pin. Add one line that says which binding type you kept and why.

CQ36.brief: Sequencer has a keyboard shortcut for almost every common action. When you know the shortcuts, you work much faster than with the toolbar buttons. In this quest you go through playback, keying, key editing and section editing with the keyboard only, and you write down what each shortcut did.
checklist: Open any sequence that has a camera and a mesh. Do this whole quest without the toolbar buttons wherever a hotkey exists.

Practice playback. Press Space to play, Up Arrow to jump to the start, and Ctrl + Up Arrow to jump to the end. Press L and J to shuttle forward and backward, and press comma and period to step between keys.
Set the playback range with [ and ] at the playhead. Press Home to reframe the timeline.
Select the mesh in the viewport. Press S to key the full transform. Then move the mesh and press Shift + W to key only the Location.
Select two keys and press 4 (Linear), then 1 (Cubic Auto). Move them by one frame with Ctrl + Right Arrow. Then press Ctrl + M and move them by 12 frames.
Select a section, put the playhead in the middle of it, and press Ctrl + / to split it. Trim the pieces with Ctrl + , and Ctrl + . (comma and period).

Drag a new actor into the level while you hold Shift, then drag another one while you hold Ctrl. Check which one became a spawnable in Sequencer. Then drag the playhead with MMB to move the time without evaluating the sequence.
CQ36.done_when: Send a short writeup of 8 to 12 lines that lists each hotkey you used and what it did. Also send one screenshot that shows the split section and the two actors that were added as a spawnable and as a possessable.
